chunks: 34 - We were informed by Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sa'id who said: Abu Sulayman Ahmad ibn Hawtha al-Bahili narrated to us, who said: Ibrahim ibn Ishaq al-Nahawandi narrated to us in Nahawand in the year 273 AH, who said: Abdullah ibn Hammad al-Ansari narrated to us in the month of Ramadan in the year 229 AH, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying:

This matter, which you stretch your necks towards, will not come to pass until a caller from the Heaven calls out: 'Behold, so-and-so is the Master of the Matter (the Imam), so for what reason is there fighting?'

key_terms.الْأَمْرُ: The matter/authority (referring to the Imamate or the Mahdi's leadership)
key_terms.الْقِتَالُ: Fighting/struggle (referring to the conflicts over leadership)
key_terms.صَاحِبُ الْأَمْرِ: The Master of the Matter (a title for the Imam/Mahdi)
key_terms.مُنَادٍ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ: A caller from the Heaven (a divine announcer in the end times)

ai.seo_question: What is the sign of the caller from heaven in Shia eschatology?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him), recorded by al-Nu'mani, the 'calling from the heavens' (Nida') serves as a definitive divine sign that terminates the era of political ambiguity and human contention for authority. This event marks the transition from the occultation to the visible leadership of the Mahdi, establishing his legitimacy through direct celestial proclamation rather than human selection. It underscores the Shia belief that true governance is a divine appointment, rendering all competing claims to power ultimately futile.

en.abdullah-al-shahin: (43) Ahmad bin Muhammad bin Sa’eed narrated from Abu Sulayman Ahmad bin Hawtha al-Bahili from Ibraheem bin Iss’haq an-Nahawandi from Abullah bin Hammad al-Ansari from Abdulla bin Sinan that Abu Abdulla as-Sadiq (as) had said: “
This matter, which you stretch your necks to, will not be until a caller from the Heaven calls: “So and so is the man of this matter so what is this fighting for?”
